newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat war crimes indictee may surrender - paper.
newsitem.headline: Croat war crimes indictee may surrender - paper.

text.p: The most prominent Bosnian Croat indicted for war crimes would give himself up to the Hague tribunal if guaranteed a trial in a "reasonable" period of time, a top Bosnian official told a news magazine on Wednesday.

The case of Dario Kordic, the most wanted Bosnian Croat indictee, "could be resolved relatively quickly", Kresimir Zubak, the Croat member of Bosnia's collective presidency, told the Zagreb-based political weekly Globus.
Zubak said in an interview in this week's issue of Globus that representatives of the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia (ICTY) were establishing contacts with Kordic's family.

"I think it is possible to reach an agreement for (Kordic) to hand himself over to the Hague tribunal on the condition that his trial starts in a reasonable period of time," Zubak told Globus. "I am almost sure that Kordic's case will be solved precisely in this manner -- very quickly."

The interview was the first time a high-ranking Croatian or Bosnian Croat official has openly raised the possibility of Kordic following in the footsteps of General Tihomir Blaskic -- his former military commander and also indicted by the tribunal -- who turned himself in, in April 1996.

The two men held the top civilian and military positions in the Lasva valley in central Bosnia during the 1993-94 war between Croats and Moslems. Blaskic had to wait more than 15 months for his trial to start.
Zubak's comments are the first indication that Western pressure on Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, the principal supporter of Bosnian Croats, is having results.

The United States have leaned on Tudjman, including blocking financial aid through the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, in order to force him to stick to commitments made under the Dayton peace agreement.
One of the provisions of the accord that ended the Bosnian war in 1995, was the handing over for trial of indicted war criminals who are seen as an obstacle to building a lasting peace.
Other prominent figures still at large include former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his military commander, General Ratko Mladic.
Western mediators recently said they were cautiously optimistic Tudjman would respond to pressure and perhaps deliver some of the people wanted by the tribunal.
In a joint statement issued last week after talks with Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic and U.S. peace envoy Richard Holbrooke, Tudjman appeared more ready than ever to co-operate with The Hague.
"President Tudjman will do his utmost to effect the transfer or voluntary surrender of Croat indictees currently at large to the tribunal on an urgent basis," the statement said.
Kordic and other ethnic Croats charged with war crimes were believed to have been sheltered by the Croatian government.

Last year a Zagreb-based magazine published photographs of Kordic in front of his Zagreb apartment where he was apparently living unhindered. The Croatian government denied the report and said Bosnian Croat war crimes suspects were out of its reach, at large in Bosnia.
Zubak also told Globus another Bosnian Croat wanted by the tribunal, Ivica Rajic, was believed to have left the country.
